title: Volpert Family Associate Professor of Business Administration
bio: Prof. Whillans investigates how individuals and organizations allocate time. Using a combination of field experiments, laboratory studies, and large-scale surveys, she examines the links between time-use decisions and well-being at the individual, team, and organizational levels. She also designs and tests interventions aimed at improving how people spend their time, looking at causal impacts on well-being and productivity. Her work spans three interconnected areas: (1) documenting the relationship between time-use decisions and self-reported well-being, (2) developing and testing interventions to change time-use at work and outside of it, and (3) applying behavioral insights to improve the design of workplace policies and practices. Her empirical work spans individual and organizational levels. Across 11 studies with nearly 60,000 working adults, people who make time-saving purchases with their romantic partners report greater relationship satisfaction (Whillans, Pow & Gladstone, 2025, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology ). At work, the decision to ask for more time on adjustable deadlines predicts task performance and reduced stress (Whillans et al., 2021, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences ). In collaboration with top consulting firms and technology companies, Prof. Whillans studies how manager-led time interventions and hybrid work arrangements influence individual and team-level performance and well-being.

Whillans Volpert Family Associate Professor of Business Administration Volpert Family Associate Professor of Business Administration Read more Ashley Whillans is the Volpert Family Associate Professor of Business Administration at the Harvard Business School, where she teaches the Motivation and Incentives course to MBA students. Professor Whillans earned her PhD in Social Psychology from the University of British Columbia. Her PhD research on time and happiness won the 2018 CAGS Distinguished Dissertation Award and was named the top PhD thesis in Canada across the fine arts, humanities, and social science
